Campaigns and Lasting Consequences

The company returns with the missing workers and a story the village will repeat for years. One hero returns with a scar. Another has spent the last Grit they were saving for a desperate hour. The road is open again, but the people who opened it have changed.

A campaign follows both kinds of consequence: what the heroes change in the world and what their adventures leave with them. Let victories last, let costs matter, and make room for the players to choose what comes next.

Award levels for meaningful progress

Use milestones when the heroes resolve an important problem, achieve a shared goal or reach a significant turning point. A negotiated settlement can qualify just as well as a battle. Tell the group what kind of progress you intend to recognize so they do not feel required to seek unnecessary fights.

At level 2 and every later level, award 8 + the new level DP. These points can be saved and spent in a place you judge safe. The character-creation DP adjustments from Knowledge, Reason and Guile apply only at levels 0 and 1, not to later awards.

Grit grants add the new point; they do not refund previous expenditure. Attributes and HP do not rise automatically with level. Cards may provide their explicit, limited increases. Discipline ranks are purchased in sequence at class prices, and the hero must meet a card's requirements before buying it. There are no prerequisite-card chains or access to a second class's signatures.

> Example: reaching level 3. A hero receives 11 DP, gains one Grit and chooses > a level-3 signature from their class. They can now buy eligible Adept cards, but > still need those cards' discipline requirements. Their base attributes and HP > remain the same unless a specific purchase or effect changes them.

Review the group's new choices before preparing the next adventure. A new route, healing option or area attack can change what an obstacle asks of the party. Do not immediately make every new ability ineffective; give the players a chance to enjoy the choice they made.

Safe places and downtime

A safe place is a judgment about the situation, not a magical property of an inn. A guarded camp may be safe; a room above a hostile tavern may not. Explain the reason when the party asks whether it can spend DP or take a breath. Do not move the standard simply because you hoped to keep them under pressure.

Distinguish a safe breath from longer work. HP recovery does not complete a four-hour fitting attempt, buy ingredients or advance a research project by a day. For downtime, ask each player what they do, record the required time and resources, and resolve only consequential uncertainty.

Track the wound receiving treatment, its accumulated recovery progress and whether it has had today's attempt. Track crafting by recipe and supply; track derivation by its own interval and target. Several heroes can pursue different projects, but they cannot pool group rolls into crafting, derivation or treatment.

Grit is a lasting resource

Characters begin with 2 Grit at level 1 and gain a point at levels 3 and 7. A once-only learned card can provide another. Ordinary rest does not refill it. Keep both grants and expenditure visible, so the player knows what remains when a dangerous choice arrives.

Do not use a fixed quota of encounters to grind away Grit. Give dangers understandable stakes and opportunities to prepare, negotiate or withdraw. Choosing to risk a remaining point for a companion should feel like the player's decision. A campaign can remain challenging through objectives, rivals and changed circumstances without making every journey an unavoidable sequence of fights.

When a hero reaches 0 HP

A player character enters Dying, immediately suffers a new wound, and follows the survival procedure. Ordinary creatures and NPCs die at 0 instead; they do not automatically gain the heroes' death rolls or Grit. A summoned form disappears.

Roll 3d6 plus one die per prior wound, capped at five dice total. Keep the highest three, sort them from low to high, and read them as a three-digit result. The new wound joins the count after this roll. Treatment never removes a scar from the count.

Choose the table for the largest damage component after resistance; the player chooses ties. When all components were resisted and only the minimum 1 damage causes the wound, the player chooses among the attack's original damage types. Physical includes force and sonic. Fire, Cold and Lightning share Elemental wounds but retain separate resistances. Mental, Radiant and Life/Necrotic each have a table.

> Example: the second wound. A hero with one prior wound rolls 2, 4, 4 and 6. > Keep 4, 4, 6 and read 446, not fourteen. If the attack dealt 2 Physical and > 1 Fire but both were fully resisted, the minimum damage still applies and the > player chooses Physical or Elemental for that result.

If a body part is absent or the result cannot apply, advance to the next listed result, such as 116 to 122, until an applicable entry is reached. Do not reroll for a more convenient wound. All tables end at 666.

Keep the survival choice clear

At the start of a Dying turn, the player chooses to spend one Grit or make a death roll. That choice stands for the turn; they cannot see the roll before deciding. Spending Grit restores full HP but preserves the wound.

Fortitude death rollResult
WeakAdd 1 death mark.
StandardNo change.
StrongStabilize at 0 HP and clear death marks.
Retained natural 111Add 2 death marks instead of the ordinary Weak result.
Retained natural 666Restore 1 HP and clear death marks.

At three death marks, the character enters Last Words. Damage while already Dying adds one mark per damaging event, not another wound. Damage that returns a stabilized character to Dying causes a new wound and adds one mark.

The universal Stabilize Maneuver targets an adjacent Dying PC, clears their marks and leaves them at 0 HP, unable to act. Healing above 0 clears marks and ends HP-caused unconsciousness, but does not remove an unrelated condition. A safe breath cannot be used to skip an unresolved Dying procedure.

Run this moment carefully. State the current HP, marks, Grit and relevant conditions. Other players can decide how to help, but the fallen hero's player chooses whether to spend their Grit.

Treatment removes effects, not history

Each wound identifies its lasting penalties, required treatment and Recovery Value, or RV. Use the appropriate card and its full work interval. Weak, Standard and Strong add 1/2/3 recovery progress. Each wound can receive only one treatment attempt per day across all healers.

When progress reaches RV, remove exactly the listed treatable effects. The scar and wound count remain. A separate temporary condition uses its normal decay or removal; it does not restart because the wound is still recorded.

> Example: a shoulder wound. Physical 333 applies Bleeding 1 and a lasting > Bane to physical activities. Bleeding resolves and decays, or can be reduced > appropriately. Soft Tissue treatment needs RV 3 to remove the Bane. Standard > treatment adds 2 on one day; Weak adds 1 on the next, completing treatment. > The scar remains and counts toward later wound rolls.

Use the broad language of physical or mental activities when applying wound Banes. Decide whether the injury matters to the task rather than requiring an argument about exactly which joint moved. Cosmetic and social consequences should likewise follow the entry; treatment that removes both a social Boon and Bane removes both.

A replacement limb is a real project. The Simple Replacement Leg recipe makes a prosthesis; Fit a Replacement then fits it and relieves only the penalties the wound allows it to relieve. Owning a wooden leg does not itself erase a movement penalty, regrow a limb or remove the scar. A rest remedy applies only when printed.

Last Words and what follows

A wound result of 666, or three death marks, begins Last Words. The character can speak and do nothing else. They die at the end of the second following turn. Ordinary healing, treatment, potions and Grit cannot reverse this. Only an explicit exceptional ability could say otherwise.

Give that time to the player. They may offer a warning, name a successor, speak to a friend or remain silent. Do not require a speech or turn the moment into a test of performance. Resolve any abilities triggered by hearing Last Words according to their own text.

Afterward, let the group decide what the company does. A funeral, a journey home or a promise to finish the work may matter more than immediately introducing another threat. Discuss a replacement character promptly so the player can return to active participation. Agree on entry circumstances and starting resources openly; this book does not impose an unreviewed universal replacement package.

Capture, retreat and retirement

Attacks are lethal unless an explicit ability provides a different outcome. Ordinary opponents die at 0 HP. To take a prisoner, secure surrender while they can still choose it or use grappling and restraint. Do not let an attacker declare all their lethal damage nonlethal after the outcome.

When escape is possible, describe it. Withdrawing may cost equipment, position or an objective, but those consequences should follow the scene. Do not promise safety and then invent pursuit that the opposition had no way to organize.

A player may choose retirement before death. Their hero can become a local ally, a mentor or someone the next company hopes to impress. Preserve that person's achievements without turning them into a free source of unlimited abilities or supplies. The campaign's continuity comes from its relationships and consequences, not from requiring the same four people to survive every chapter.
